Deciphering the role of Histone Modifications in Memory and Exhausted CD8 T Cells - Part 3

Florence Marti, Valerie Heckendorn

2025-07-01

9.) Comparing the hPMTs of the different cell types using enriched heatmaps

9.1) Importing the peaks from part 1

peaks_part1 <- GRangesList(
  H3K27ac = import("peak_bed_files/H3K27ac_peaks.bed"),
  H3K27me3 = import("peak_bed_files/H3K27me3_peaks.bed"),
  H3K4me3 = import("peak_bed_files/H3K4me3_peaks.bed"),
  H3K9me3 = import("peak_bed_files/H3K9me3_peaks.bed")
)

9.2) Importing the BigWig files and constructing the signal matrices for the individual cell types

# Naive
bwfiles_naive <- list.files("BW", pattern = "_naive.bw$", full.names = TRUE)
bwfiles_naive
## [1] "BW/H3K27ac_naive.bw"  "BW/H3K27me3_naive.bw" "BW/H3K4me3_naive.bw" 
## [4] "BW/H3K9me3_naive.bw"
names(bwfiles_naive) <- gsub("\\.bw$", "", basename(bwfiles_naive))
naive_regions <- reduce(unlist(GRangesList(peaks_part1)))
sm_n <- signal2Matrix(bwfiles_naive, regions = naive_regions, w = 40)
## Reading BW/H3K27ac_naive.bw
## Reading BW/H3K27me3_naive.bw
## Reading BW/H3K4me3_naive.bw
## Reading BW/H3K9me3_naive.bw
# Memory
bwfiles_memory <- list.files("BW", pattern = "_memory.bw$", full.names = TRUE)
names(bwfiles_memory) <- gsub("\\.bw$", "", basename(bwfiles_memory))
memory_regions <- reduce(unlist(GRangesList(peaks_part1)))
sm_m <- signal2Matrix(bwfiles_memory, regions = memory_regions, w = 40)
## Reading BW/H3K27ac_memory.bw
## Reading BW/H3K27me3_memory.bw
## Reading BW/H3K4me3_memory.bw
## Reading BW/H3K9me3_memory.bw
# Exhausted
bwfiles_exh <- list.files("BW", pattern = "_EX.bw$", full.names = TRUE)
names(bwfiles_exh) <- gsub("\\.bw$", "", basename(bwfiles_exh))
exh_regions <- reduce(unlist(GRangesList(peaks_part1)))
sm_e <- signal2Matrix(bwfiles_exh, regions = exh_regions, w = 40)
## Reading BW/H3K27ac_EX.bw
## Reading BW/H3K27me3_EX.bw
## Reading BW/H3K4me3_EX.bw
## Reading BW/H3K9me3_EX.bw

9.3) Filtering

Using only the top 5000 hits of the signal matrices, due to processing power of the computers used.

sm_m1 <- sm_m[1:5000,]
sm_n1 <- sm_n[1:5000,]
sm_e1<- sm_e[1:5000,]

9.4) Plotting the enriched heatmaps for the filtered signal matrices

9.4.1) Naïve T-cells

plotEnrichedHeatmaps(sm_n1, multiScale = T, cluster_rows = T, show_row_dend = T)

Figure 7. Enriched heatmaps of histone modifications at genomic regions in naïve T-cells. Heatmaps display the enrichment of four histone modifications—H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me3, and H3K9me3—across genomic regions centered at defined loci (center, dashed line), spanning ±2 kb. Each row represents an individual genomic region, clustered by signal intensity. The color scale indicates the normalised ChIP-seq signal for each modification, as shown by the color bars on the right. Above each heatmap, the average signal profile (red line) with shaded confidence intervals summarises enrichment patterns across all regions.

H3K27ac and H3K4me3 are sharply enriched at the centre of the regions, suggesting these sites are active promoters or enhancers in naïve T-cells. In contrast, H3K27me3 shows low signal overall, with some enrichment at specific sites, in line with its role as a repressive mark. H3K9me3 is mostly absent from the centre but appears at a distinct subset of regions, reflecting its link to heterochromatin and gene silencing. The clustering points to clearly different chromatin states, with active and repressive marks rarely overlapping.

9.4.2) Memory T-cells

plotEnrichedHeatmaps(sm_m1,  multiScale = T, cluster_rows = T, show_row_dend = T)

Figure 8. Enriched heatmap of histone modifications at genomic regions in memory T-cells. Heatmaps display the enrichment of four histone modifications—H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me3, and H3K9me3—across genomic regions centred at defined loci (centre, dashed line), spanning ±2 kb. Each row represents an individual genomic region, clustered by signal intensity. The colour scale indicates the normalised ChIP-seq signal for each modification, as shown by the colour bars on the right. Above each heatmap, the average signal profile (red line) with shaded confidence intervals summarises enrichment patterns across all regions

In memory T-cells, H3K27ac and H3K4me3 remain strongly enriched at the centre of the regions, marking active promoters and enhancers. H3K27me3 shows a more complex pattern than in naïve T-cells, with clear central enrichment at some sites and additional peaks on either side, pointing to changes in how repressive chromatin is organised. H3K9me3 is enriched both at the centre and flanking regions in certain loci, suggesting that heterochromatin forms at specific genomic sites during memory T-cell differentiation. Clustering reveals distinct chromatin states, and in some regions, active and repressive marks appear together — particularly noticeable in the H3K27me3 pattern.

9.4.3) Exhausted T-cells

plotEnrichedHeatmaps(sm_e1,  multiScale = T, cluster_rows = T, show_row_dend = T)

Figure 9. Heatmaps and average profiles of histone modifications at genomic regions in exhausted T-cells. Heatmaps display the enrichment of four histone modifications—H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me3, and H3K9me3—across genomic regions centred at defined loci (centre, dashed line), spanning ±2 kb. Each row represents an individual genomic region, clustered by signal intensity as shown in the dendrogram on the left. The colour scales indicate the normalised ChIP-seq signal for each modification. Above each heatmap, the average signal profile (red line) with shaded confidence intervals summarises enrichment patterns across all regions.

In exhausted T-cells, H3K27ac and H3K4me3 remain enriched at the centre of regions, suggesting that active regulatory elements are still marked, although the strength of these signals may differ from other T-cell states. H3K27me3 shows a distinct pattern, with moderate central enrichment and additional flanking signal, hinting at a more complex repressive chromatin landscape. H3K9me3 stands out with a striking redistribution, showing strong enrichment in specific clusters of regions — consistent with widespread heterochromatin formation and gene silencing in the exhausted state. Clustering highlights clear chromatin signatures, with regions separating based on their histone mark profiles, most notably through the patterns of H3K9me3.

9.5) Clustering

9.5.1) Finding the best kmeans for clustering of the samples

cl_n <- clusterSignalMatrices(sm_n1, k=2:7)
cluster1 <- ggplot(cl_n$varExplained, aes(k, varExplained)) + geom_line() + labs(x = "Number of Clusters (k)", y = "Variance Explained") + ggtitle("A) Cluster Signal Matrix Naive T-Cells")  + theme_minimal()

cl_m <- clusterSignalMatrices(sm_m1, k=2:7)
cluster2 <- ggplot(cl_m$varExplained, aes(k, varExplained)) + geom_line() + labs(x = "Number of Clusters (k)", y = "Variance Explained") + ggtitle("B) Cluster Signal Matrix Memory T-Cells") + theme_minimal()

cl_e <- clusterSignalMatrices(sm_e1, k=2:7)
cluster3 <- ggplot(cl_e$varExplained, aes(k, varExplained)) + geom_line() + labs(x = "Number of Clusters (k)", y = "Variance Explained")+ ggtitle("C) Cluster Signal Matrix Exhausted T-Cells") + theme_minimal()
grid.arrange(cluster1, cluster2, cluster3,
             ncol = 1,
             top = "K-Means Clustering: Variance Explained per k")

Figure 10. K-means clustering: Variance Explained by k for all three T-cell types: A) naive T-cells, B) memory T-cells, C) exhausted T-cells. x-axis visualises the numbers of clusters producced ranging from 2-7 clusters, y-axis shows the corresponding variance that is explained by these clusters.

In all 3 cell types we see a similar pattern of increase of the variance explained by increasing the clusters. For all three groups the same amount of clusters (k= 6) was chosen for further analysis.

9.5.2) Setting the clusters

set.seed(123)  # to ensure that it gives the same results everytime
cl_k_n <- clusterSignalMatrices(sm_n1, k=6)
##   ~95% of the variance explained by clusters
cl_k_m <- clusterSignalMatrices(sm_m1, k=6)
##   ~94% of the variance explained by clusters
cl_k_e <- clusterSignalMatrices(sm_e1, k=6)
##   ~96% of the variance explained by clusters

using k = 6 we have an average 95% of the variance explained.

Adding clusters to the signal matrices and plotting the enriched heatmaps

rowData(sm_n1)$cluster <- cl_k_n
rowData(sm_m1)$cluster <- cl_k_m
rowData(sm_e1)$cluster <- cl_k_e

mycolors <- c("1"="pink", "2"="lightblue", "3"="darkgreen", "4"="orange", "5"="purple", "6"="blue")
plotEnrichedHeatmaps(sm_n1, row_split="cluster", mean_color=mycolors, colors=c("white","darkred"))

Figure 11. Enriched heatmaps of histone modifications at clustered genomic regions in naïve T-cells. Heatmaps showing the distribution of H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me3, and H3K9me3 signals (±2 kb from centre, dashed line) for six region clusters. Active marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me3) are enriched at the centre in clusters 2,3,4, and 5, while repressive marks (H3K27me3, H3K9me3) are largely absent. Average signal profiles are shown above each heatmap. 

plotEnrichedHeatmaps(sm_m1, row_split="cluster", mean_color=mycolors, colors=c("white","darkred"))

Figure 12. Enriched heatmaps of histone modifications at clustered genomic regions in memory T-cells. Heatmaps showing the distribution of H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me3, and H3K9me3 signals (±2 kb from centre, dashed line) for six region clusters. Active marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me3) are enriched at the centre in clusters 1,2,4, and 6, while repressive mark H3K27me3 is enriched at the centre in cluster 3. H3K9me3 is largely absent. Average signal profiles are shown above each heatmap. 

plotEnrichedHeatmaps(sm_e1, row_split="cluster", mean_color=mycolors, colors=c("white","darkred"))

Figure 13. Enriched heatmaps of histone modifications at clustered genomic regions in exhausted T-cells. Heatmaps showing the distribution of H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me3, and H3K9me3 signals (±2 kb from centre, dashed line) for six region clusters. Active marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me3) are enriched at the centre in clusters 1,3,4, and 6, while repressive mark H3K27me3 is enriched at the centre in cluster 2. H3K9me3 is largely absent. Average signal profiles are shown above each heatmap. 

naive <- meltSignals(sm_n1, splitBy=cl_k_n)
memory <- meltSignals(sm_m1, splitBy=cl_k_m)
exhausted <- meltSignals(sm_e1, splitBy=cl_k_e)

melt1 <- ggplot(naive, aes(position, mean, colour=sample)) + geom_line(size=1.2) + facet_wrap(~split) + ggtitle("A) Naive T-Cells")
## Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
## ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.
## This warning is displayed once every 8 hours.
## Call `lifecycle::last_lifecycle_warnings()` to see where this warning was
## generated.
melt2 <- ggplot(memory, aes(position, mean, colour=sample)) + geom_line(size=1.2) + facet_wrap(~split) + ggtitle("B) Memory T-Cells")
melt3 <- ggplot(exhausted, aes(position, mean, colour=sample)) + geom_line(size=1.2) + facet_wrap(~split) + ggtitle("C) Exhausted T-Cells")
plot_grid(melt1, melt2, melt3, ncol = 1)

Figure 14. Average profiles of histone modifications across six genomic region clusters in A) naïve T-cells, B) memory T-cells, and C) exhausted T-cells. Line plots show mean signal for H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me3, and H3K9me3 (±2 kb from centre, position 0) in each cluster. A) Clusters 2, 4, and 5 display strong central enrichment of active marks (H3K4me3, H3K27ac), while repressive mark H3K27me3 presents a low across enrichment in cluster 1. H3K9me3 is absent in all clusters. B) Clusters 1, 4, and 6 show strong central enrichment for active marks, while cluster 3 shows strong central enrichment for H2K27me3 repression. C) Clusters 1, 4, and 6 showing strong enrichment for active marks, and cluster 3 showing mild enrichment for active marks. Cluster 2 showing mild enrichment for repressive mark H3K27me3.

10.) GO Analysis

10.1) Annotating the peaks of one of the clusters per hPMT

For the annotation, the mm10 known genes are used, identical to what was used in the original publication.

txdb <- TxDb.Mmusculus.UCSC.mm10.knownGene

sm_n1_cluster5 <- sm_n1[rowData(sm_n1)$cluster == 5]
sm_m1_cluster4 <- sm_m1[rowData(sm_m1)$cluster == 4]
sm_e1_cluster1 <- sm_e1[rowData(sm_e1)$cluster == 1]

anno_n_cluster5 <- annotatePeak(rowRanges(sm_n1_cluster5), TxDb = txdb, annoDb = "org.Mm.eg.db", tssRegion = c(-3000, 3000), verbose = FALSE)
## 'select()' returned 1:many mapping between keys and columns
anno_m_cluster4 <- annotatePeak(rowRanges(sm_m1_cluster4), TxDb = txdb, annoDb = "org.Mm.eg.db", tssRegion = c(-3000, 3000), verbose = FALSE)
## 'select()' returned 1:many mapping between keys and columns
anno_e_cluster1 <- annotatePeak(rowRanges(sm_e1_cluster1), TxDb = txdb, annoDb = "org.Mm.eg.db", tssRegion = c(-3000, 3000), verbose = FALSE)
## 'select()' returned 1:1 mapping between keys and columns
genes_n1_cluster5 <- unique(na.omit(anno_n_cluster5@anno$geneId))
genes_m1_cluster4 <- unique(na.omit(anno_m_cluster4@anno$geneId))
genes_e1_cluster1 <- unique(na.omit(anno_e_cluster1@anno$geneId))

10.2) GO-analysing the clusters

GO_n_cluster5 <- enrichGO(gene = genes_n1_cluster5, OrgDb = org.Mm.eg.db, keyType = "ENTREZID", ont = "BP", pAdjustMethod = "BH", qvalueCutoff = 0.05, readable = TRUE)
GO_m_cluster4 <- enrichGO(gene = genes_m1_cluster4, OrgDb = org.Mm.eg.db, keyType = "ENTREZID", ont = "BP", pAdjustMethod = "BH", qvalueCutoff = 0.05, readable = TRUE)
GO_e_cluster1 <- enrichGO(gene = genes_e1_cluster1, OrgDb = org.Mm.eg.db, keyType = "ENTREZID", ont = "BP", pAdjustMethod = "BH", qvalueCutoff = 0.05, readable = TRUE)

10.2.1) plotting

truncate_words <- function(x, n = 5) {
  sapply(strsplit(x, " "), function(words) paste(head(words, n), collapse = " "))
}

# Naive cluster 1
top_n_cluster5 <- as.data.frame(GO_n_cluster5) %>%
  slice_head(n = 50) %>%
  mutate(
    Group = "Naive Cluster 5",
    fold_enrichment = sapply(strsplit(GeneRatio, "/"), function(x) as.numeric(x[1]) / as.numeric(x[2])),
    observed_region_hits = Count,
    short_description = truncate_words(Description, n = 5),
    p_adjust = p.adjust
  )

# Memory cluster 4
top_m_cluster4 <- as.data.frame(GO_m_cluster4) %>%
  slice_head(n = 50) %>%
  mutate(
    Group = "Memory Cluster 4",
    fold_enrichment = sapply(strsplit(GeneRatio, "/"), function(x) as.numeric(x[1]) / as.numeric(x[2])),
    observed_region_hits = Count,
    short_description = truncate_words(Description, n = 5),
    p_adjust = p.adjust
  )

# Exhausted cluster 5
top_e_cluster1 <- as.data.frame(GO_e_cluster1) %>%
  slice_head(n = 50) %>%
  mutate(
    Group = "Exhausted Cluster 1",
    fold_enrichment = sapply(strsplit(GeneRatio, "/"), function(x) as.numeric(x[1]) / as.numeric(x[2])),
    observed_region_hits = Count,
    short_description = truncate_words(Description, n = 5),
    p_adjust = p.adjust
  )
top10_n <- top_n_cluster5 %>%
  arrange(p_adjust) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

ggplot(top10_n, aes(fold_enrichment, reorder(short_description, fold_enrichment),
                      size = observed_region_hits, color = -log10(p_adjust))) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_viridis_c() +
  labs(
    x = "Fold Enrichment", y = "GO Term (Naive)",
    title = "Naive T-cell Cluster 5 GO Enrichment",
    size = "Gene Count", color = "-log10(p.adjust)"
  ) + theme_minimal()

Figure 15. GO enrichment analysis of genomic regions in cluster 5 for naïve T-cells. Bubble plots display the 50 top enriched Biological Process terms for each cluster based on annotated genes within +/- 3kb of the TSS. The x-axis shows fold enrichement (gene ratio), bubble size indicates number of region-associated genes contributing to the term, and color represents statistical significance (-log10 adjusted p-value).

Here, naïve T-cell cluster 5 is enriched for terms associated with adaptive immune regulation and development. Notably, the GO output also includes broad or non specific terms, such as “positive regulation of hydrolase activity”, which are not directly related to T-cell function. These may arise due to the general nature of some GO categories, highlighting the importance of biological interpretation beyond statistical analysis alone.

The x-axis shows fold enrichement (gene ratio), bubble size indicates number of region-associated genes contributing to the term, and color represents statistical significance (-log10 adjusted p-value).

Here, memory T-cell cluster 4 is enriched for terms on T cell activation and regulation.

ggplot(top10_e, aes(fold_enrichment, reorder(short_description, fold_enrichment),

Figure 17. GO enrichment analysis of genomic regions in cluster 1 for exhausted T-cells. Bubble plots display the 50 top enriched Biological Process terms for each cluster based on annotated genes within +/- 3kb of the TSS. The x-axis shows fold enrichement (gene ratio), bubble size indicates number of region-associated genes contributing to the term, and color represents statistical significance (-log10 adjusted p-value).

The exhausted T-cell cluster is enriched in terms of the positive regulation of lymphocyte and leukocyte activation.

11.) Conclusion

Our analysis reveals how the chromatin landscape shifts as CD8+ T-cells transition from naïve to memory and eventually to an exhausted state. Naïve T-cells display a clean, activation-ready profile, with strong enrichment of active marks (H3K27ac, H3K4me3) and minimal repressive signals. In memory T-cells, the landscape becomes more layered: active marks remain at key sites, but repressive modifications spread more broadly, reflecting increased regulatory complexity. Exhausted T-cells show the most dramatic changes, with dense clusters of H3K9me3 forming distinct heterochromatic regions. Although active marks persist, the rise in repressive signals—particularly the loss of bivalent states and the dominance of H3K9me3—marks a fundamental shift toward gene silencing.

Clustering analysis (k=6) identified distinct chromatin states across the T-cell differentiation stages, with exhaustion-specific clusters enriched for genes involved in viral responses. The emergence of heterochromatic foci in these cells reflects a spatial reorganisation of the genome that aligns with their impaired function under chronic antigen exposure. These findings show that epigenetic reprogramming is not just about changes in histone mark levels—it also involves shifts in 3D genome architecture, linking chromatin structure directly to T-cell dysfunction.

Our GO anaylsis reveals that epigenetic reprogramming during CD8+ T-cell differentiation involves not only changes in histone mark levels but also reorganisation of the genome, with distinct functional effects at each stage. Naïve T-cells have focused active chromatin structures, with gene functions linked to adaptive immune regulation despite some broad biological terms. Memory T-cells develop more layered chromatin domains, reflected in gene functions related to T-cell activation and flexibility. Exhausted T-cells undergo extensive heterochromatin formation, creating H3K9me3-rich regions enriched for viral response genes—tying 3D genome changes directly to their impaired function during chronic antigen exposure.

Together, these findings show that exhaustion involves both quantitative shifts in histone marks and qualitative changes in chromatin architecture. The clustering of repressive marks into defined genomic compartments provides a structural explanation for the transcriptional dysfunction seen in exhausted T-cells, highlighting new targets for therapeutic intervention in chronic disease.
